Is this rental a good deal? One number can't tell you. Here are the five that can, using an example: a two hundred fifty thousand dollar house renting for twenty four hundred a month.

Number one, cash flow. A year of rent is twenty eight thousand eight hundred. Take out vacancy and operating costs, and net operating income is about nineteen thousand nine hundred. The mortgage takes about fourteen thousand six hundred. What's left is cash flow: five thousand two hundred eighty seven a year, or four hundred forty one dollars a month.

Number two, cap rate. That's net operating income divided by the purchase price. Nineteen thousand nine hundred over two hundred fifty thousand is seven point nine five percent. It shows how the property performs, no matter how you finance it.

Number three, cash on cash return. That's your yearly cash flow divided by the cash you actually put in. Five thousand two hundred eighty seven over seventy thousand is seven point five five percent. This one shows how hard your own money is working.

Number four, D S C R, the debt service coverage ratio. That's net operating income divided by your mortgage payments. Here it's one point three six. Many lenders want about one point two five or higher, so this deal clears that bar.

Number five, the one percent rule. Monthly rent divided by price. Twenty four hundred over two hundred fifty thousand is zero point nine six percent, just under one percent. But this house still cash flows. The rule is a quick filter, not a verdict.

So is it a good deal? No single number decides it. Cash flow, cap rate, cash on cash, D S C R, and the one percent rule each tell part of the story. Look at all five together, and test what happens if rent or rates change.
